narrative:
Your loan application was reviewed by an automated credit assessment system, which predicted a 51% probability that you represent a bad credit risk — a result that sits right on the borderline, but was still enough to result in a denial. This is an important detail: your situation is not a clear-cut rejection, and the model's decision hinges on a relatively narrow margin, which means targeted changes to your profile could realistically tip the outcome in your favor.

To understand why the application was denied and what could change that outcome, it helps to think in terms of "what if" scenarios — alternative versions of your profile that would have led to an approval. These counterfactual scenarios don't change who you are, but they highlight which aspects of your financial profile the model weighs most heavily when making its decision.

Across all three alternative scenarios generated for your case, every single one required exactly one change: the status of your checking account. In your current profile, your checking account shows a negative balance, meaning it is overdrawn. In every scenario where the model would have approved your application, this was changed to reflect no checking account at all — which, perhaps counterintuitively, the model treats more favorably than an account in the red. This is the single most decisive factor in your denial, and it changed in 100% of the counterfactual scenarios, while all other 16 features — including your loan amount, duration, employment, savings, and housing — remained completely unchanged across every scenario.

This finding is striking because your other financial characteristics are not particularly alarming on their own. Your requested loan amount of 1,108 DM is actually well below the average of approximately 2,887 DM among applicants who were approved, and your 12-month repayment duration is shorter than the approved applicant average of about 19 months — both of which suggest a relatively modest and manageable request. You own your home, have stable employment of 4 to 7 years, and have no other debtors or co-applicants involved, all of which align reasonably well with the profiles of approved applicants.

However, a few other features in your profile do place you in a less favorable position compared to approved applicants, even if they weren't the deciding factor here. Your installment rate — the share of your disposable income going toward repayments — is 4%, compared to an average of about 2.94% among approved applicants, meaning your repayments consume a larger portion of your income. You also have 2 existing credits at this bank, compared to an average of 1.42 among approved applicants, which signals a somewhat higher existing debt load. Your credit history category of "no credits or all paid" is also relatively rare among approved applicants, where only about 2.3% share this category, with the majority having a history of existing paid credits.

The most actionable insight from this analysis is clear: resolving the negative balance in your checking account is the single change that, according to all three modeled scenarios, would be sufficient to flip the prediction to an approval. If you are able to bring your checking account out of overdraft — even to a zero or closed status — the model's assessment of your application would likely change. Given that your loan request is modest and your employment situation is stable, addressing this one financial signal appears to be the most direct path toward a successful reapplication.
